title: AI guidance: Stop with the frameworks. Start drawing lines.
author: Michelle Brown
summary: Michelle Brown argues that education is awash in frameworks for thinking about AI but has almost no concrete guardrails telling districts and teachers what to do, and that existing policy has no pedagogical foundation. She says teachers are being asked to sift through noise while AI is tested on nine-year-olds before adults know how to use it. Strong guidance, in her view, has four traits: it must be discipline-specific, with explicit instructional guardrails, sensitive to age, and measurable in months rather than years. For English Language Arts she proposes three levels of checks, starting with alignment to knowledge-building materials, moving to whether the tool holds the bar and respects screen limits, and ending with whether it increases reading, writing, discussion, teacher confidence, and student well-being. She suggests starting with adult workflows that return time to teachers, then older students, and calls for free, valid, rapid common assessments so schools can tell quickly whether kids are learning.
points: Frameworks from the Department of Education, Brookings, and states offer ways to think about AI but no real guardrails against instructional slop.
Good AI guidance must be discipline-specific because reading and learning differ across subjects, and vendors have no profit motive to specialize.
Principals need a compact walkthrough checklist with look-fors that show in five minutes whether AI is helping or hurting instruction.
Schools should start with adult workflows that reduce teacher paperwork, then older students, before putting AI in front of young children.
Free, valid, rapid, common assessments are needed so districts learn within months whether an AI tool is changing outcomes.
quotes: AI is evolving faster than we can evaluate it. We can’t afford another vague framework. It’s time to start drawing lines in the sand.
We’re testing AI on nine-year-olds before most of the adults in the building have a concrete sense of how we should be using it for actual day-to-day instruction.
We don’t need to be shy about saying that an algorithm-driven recommendation engine isn’t instruction. It’s YouTube. What we need is expertise and courage.
AI is the world’s biggest mirror. It is trained to key off the input it is given.
What principals and teachers need is something actionable and compact: a walkthrough checklist with the look-fors that tell you in five minutes whether AI is helping or hurting.
The problem with every AI pilot running in American classrooms today is that we have no fast, reliable way to know if it’s working.
When it comes down to it, AI guidance has four jobs: get specific to the subject, hold the instructional bar, account for the child’s age and tell us quickly whether kids are actually learning.
